title: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
paragraphs: I am 篠田諭, a sixth-year student in the Department of Medicine, Nagoya University School of Medicine. I studied abroad for two months at the Chinese University of Hong Kong in Hong Kong, China. Hong Kong was ruled by the United Kingdom until 1997, and British culture can still be seen in many places. The name of the Chinese University of Hong Kong's affiliated hospital is Prince of Wales Hospital, and even this alone gives a glimpse of the traces of the colonial era. Incidentally, those who know world history well may recall, on hearing Prince of Wales, the name of a main battleship of the British Navy in the Second World War.

My accommodation in Hong Kong was a student dormitory adjacent to the hospital. Because it is mainly used by local medical students, exchange students inevitably share rooms. I spent the two months together with 近藤優樹 from the same Nagoya University. Naturally I had never spent such a long time with anyone other than family, and I felt a little uneasy. Fortunately, however, that turned out to be needless worry. Of course a certain amount of consideration was necessary, but I was rather able to have a good time. He is now my best friend.

I was looked after for one month each in otorhinolaryngology and obstetrics and gynecology. The otorhinolaryngology department of the Chinese University of Hong Kong is run by nine staff members, headed by a British professor, and treats conditions from nasal cavity diseases to hearing loss and head and neck cancer. All the staff were very educational and taught me enthusiastically. This point is the same as in clinical clerkships in Japan. I was asked a number of questions, and among them NPC was memorable. Do you know NPC? When I asked, I was told that NPC is an abbreviation for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and I could work out that it literally means nasal-pharyngeal cancer?, but I had no idea. The doctor said it is quite a major cancer in Hong Kong. When I returned to the dormitory and looked it up, it was cancer of the epipharynx (nasopharynx), and indeed it is said to be common in Southeast Asia and southern China. Now that it was pointed out, there was a constant stream of NPC patients on the ward and in the outpatient clinic, and I realized that it is indeed common. Furthermore, because Epstein-Barr virus and family history can be risk factors for nasopharyngeal cancer, in Hong Kong the presence or absence of EB virus infection and family history of nasopharyngeal cancer were routinely recorded. Being able to feel on one's skin diseases and responses specific to the locale like this is the real pleasure of studying abroad. The one month in otorhinolaryngology was over in a flash.

In ENT there were also many local medical students doing clerkships. In Hong Kong there are only two universities with medical schools, the University of Hong Kong and the Chinese University. Moreover, given the large population for the land and the high land prices, a place where only the middle class and above can live, and the enthusiastic investment in education, the people who can enter medical school are inevitably unmistakable elites. Their medical knowledge and English fluency were incomparable to those of Japanese medical students. But they were very friendly and got along very well with me, who spoke clumsy English. As I was feeling uneasy in a foreign land, I remember I was very happy. Interaction with local medical students is also something unique to studying abroad, I think.

The next month was obstetrics and gynecology. The obstetrics and gynecology department of the Chinese University was very thriving across a wide range, from departments also seen in Japan, such as oncology and perinatology, to departments relatively rare in Japan, such as infertility treatment, female urology and prenatal diagnosis. However, being thriving and being taught are different things. Unfortunately the doctors in oncology, female urology and perinatology were busy and had no time to attend to students from overseas. It was common, even on morning rounds, that they greeted me but did not come back. What would you do in such a situation? I completely ignored the schedule distributed beforehand and, on my own, observed operations that interested me and the infertility treatment clinic, which was not included in the schedule at all. Incidentally, infertility treatment in Hong Kong is famous, and the treatment results were clearly better than in Japan. The doctors, perhaps having time to spare, were also quite educational, and it was all good. As I spent my time freely like this, I entered the last week with only prenatal diagnosis remaining. The main work of prenatal diagnosis is to find congenital malformations and chromosomal abnormalities before birth. Now, in Japan you may occasionally see people with Down syndrome. Looking back, in the two months in Hong Kong I did not see a person with Down syndrome even once. The cause is Hong Kong's prenatal diagnosis. In Hong Kong, as screening for Down syndrome, nuchal translucency (NT), the edema at the back of the fetal neck, is measured in all cases at 11 to 13 weeks of pregnancy. Pregnant women suspected of Down syndrome as a result undergo amniocentesis and obtain a definitive diagnosis. When this happens almost all pregnant women choose abortion, and as a result Down syndrome is weeded out in Hong Kong. It was clearly a different ethical outlook from Japan, and I was utterly astonished. What do you think of the rights and wrongs of this? They said, "Rather, why doesn't Japan even test for Down syndrome? It is obviously abnormal." I could only reply, "We can't do it ethically." I can still remember their unconvinced faces. In Hong Kong it is common to invest huge sums in the education of one child, and that they cannot afford to raise a child from whom a corresponding return can hardly be expected may be one cause of this disagreement. Being able to feel differences in treatment policy that come from such differences in ethical outlook is also an experience that can be tasted only by studying abroad.
